context_facts: Primary report: word/nonword classification, category-name primes and neutral xxx; expectancy is separated from semantic relatedness by instructed shifts to a different category. SOAs are 250, 400, 700, and 2000 ms across groups.

Related category-exemplar facilitation occurs at short SOA; an expected but unrelated category gains facilitation later; an unexpected related target changes from facilitation to inhibition as SOA increases. The broad related/unrelated difference is embedded in these specific expectancy and timing conditions.

context_facts: Primary abstract reports five visual serial-recall experiments with irrelevant spoken sentences ending in expected versus unexpected words. Unexpected endings disrupt serial recall more.

Phonologically expected but semantically unexpected endings also disrupt recall. The semantic mismatch effect does not diminish with repeated exposure in the five experiments. Exact participant counts and experiment-specific procedures are not supplied by this abstract.

context_facts: Only metadata and a secondary indexed abstract were obtained; publisher HTML returned HTTP 403 challenge. The indexed abstract describes two experiments examining habituation of the semantic mismatch effect in visual-verbal serial recall.

Indexed account: Experiment 1 uses more trials than the original; Experiment 2 contrasts sixteen different distractor sentences with one sentence repeated sixteen times. Overall recall improves for repeated sentences while the mismatch difference remains unchanged. This is an indexed account, not a directly read primary methods section.

priming.empirical_contrast: H6 is faster mean correct visual lexical-decision RT for target words after related rather than unrelated primes. The authors expressly describe replication, cite de Groot 1984/1987 and Neely 1967/1977 together, and describe reliability of procedure/statistics/participant seriousness as its purpose.
priming.year_discrepancy: The in-text Neely 1967 is retained as printed. The bibliography uniquely supplies the matching 1976 facilitatory/inhibitory paper; it is not a verified 1967 report.
priming.task_source: The current authors expressly say Matzke et al. (2015) supplied the task and stimuli and that the task was taken from that report. Their reference is The effect of horizontal eye movements on free recall: A preregistered adversarial collaboration, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General 144(1), e1–e15, six authors as preserved in the current printed reference. Current source does not print a DOI for that entry.
priming.closest_chain_limit: Matzke is the directly identified task/materials source, closer procedurally than the four older examples. Its primary report was not acquired: one explicitly guessed author-site PDF returned 404. No primary Matzke sample, effect size, SOA, related-pair proportion, trial count, nonword composition, or cohort equivalence has been verified. This contextual report is not a seventh requested original.
priming.relation_to_older_findings: A related/unrelated RT test bears on basic facilitation differences under its actual conditions. It does not by itself recreate de Groot’s proportion×SOA pattern, de Groot’s task/nonword-composition changes, Neely’s neutral-baseline facilitation versus inhibition decomposition, or Neely’s expectancy×relatedness×SOA dissociation. Reliability purpose does not determine the scientific eligibility of the empirical comparison.

shadowing.contrast: Current authors jointly attribute disruption from unexpected sentence endings during serial recall to Röer et al. 2019 and Röer/Buchner/Bell in press, then test semantic expectation within an auditory selective-listening task.
shadowing.manipulation: Within-participant own/yoked-control name and expected/unexpected sentence-final word. Each participant’s unexpected word is the yoked partner’s expected word. Four critical words occur at minutes 3,4,5,6, onset-synchronized to relevant words with matching syllable counts; eight counterbalanced orders. Proverb examples are Arbeit/Vergnügen versus Arbeit/Späne and Liebe/Magen versus Liebe/Kraft as preserved in the appendix.
shadowing.measurement: Experimenter records shadowing errors; errors analyzed at relevant word positions −1,0,+1,+2,+3 relative to critical irrelevant word. Retrospective questionnaire follows. Semantic-expectation×position repeated-measures model yields BF10 0.060 for semantic expectation. One participant reports an unexpected word after a specific prompt without remembering which word; two report expected words.
shadowing.authors_scope_statement: Discussion explicitly says cross-modal findings cannot be generalized to a situation with both sources presented auditorily. It discusses continuous streams, critical-word salience/timing, focal task demands and working-memory capacity as possible boundary conditions. These are authors’ explanations rather than separately tested causal comparisons.
shadowing.relation_limit: Task/modality and dependent variable differ from visual serial recall. The current source nevertheless makes an empirical expected/unexpected comparison and expressly discusses generalization of prior findings; changed task and extension language alone do not settle eligibility. Attribution to the in-press co-citation is less direct than to the five-experiment paper, which is cited again in discussion.

report_chain_context.Neely: 1977 pp.230–231 expressly reviews 1976 as a prior experiment, gives its 360/600/2000-ms timing, primary-associate examples, and neutral/related/unrelated conditions; then says the present research elaborates that paradigm to separate expectancy from semantic relatedness. Thus the new report contains described design changes, not simply a different DOI/year. It is based on a Yale dissertation (p.227 acknowledgment). 122 tested, two discarded, leaving 120 across a 24-person 2000-alone group and three 32-person mixed-SOA groups. This does not establish whether any person also participated in the 1976 study, nor link the dissertation to a separately inspected dataset.
report_chain_context.Roer: Primary 2019 abstract describes five experiments, including a semantic-versus-phonological mismatch comparison and repeated-exposure analyses. The indexed Stable Effects abstract says it critically examines the prior nonhabituation finding with two experiments: more trials in Experiment 1; different versus repeatedly identical sentence in Experiment 2. The Stable Effects publisher-deposited reference list includes 10.1037/xlm0000596 at CIT0065. These concrete descriptions and the reference link counter a simple title/DOI-only conflation. However only the earlier abstract is directly primary here; the later description is secondary indexed text. Neither complete methods nor participant/data statements of these two reports were acquired, so participant overlap, data reuse, preliminary/full-report equivalence and dataset links are unresolved.
report_chain_context.in_press_identity: Matching exact title and three-author order establish the current in-press reference’s bibliographic match: Röer, Jan Philipp; Buchner, Axel; Bell, Raoul. Auditory Perception & Cognition 2(3),143–162; DOI 10.1080/25742442.2020.1722560. Crossref issue print date 2019-07-03 versus online date and publication-history assertion 2020-01-28; accepted 2020-01-21 and received 2019-04-07. Report both issue-year 2019 and online-year 2020, rather than infer the year from DOI syntax. Exact title matches current reference; shared current co-citation is not evidence that the two originals share a cohort.
